subjects.displayTitle: Teaching the Cause: the call to every believer
subjects.introduction: What do the Writings ask of every believer in teaching the Cause, and what do they say makes a word take root in another heart? These 300 chosen quotations include every verified authorized selection in the compilation. They begin with the command that every soul teach and with the worth of guiding a single soul, then turn to the instruments of teaching: wisdom and utterance in place of the sword, deeds and character before words, and the detachment of the teacher’s own heart. Later readings consider the receptivity of hearers, the prudence and concealment that circumstances once required, the confirmations promised to those who arise, the classes, meetings and consultation through which teachers are prepared, and travel in the spirit of the Tablets of the Divine Plan, before gathering accounts of those who taught and closing with prayers. Passages come from Bahá’u’lláh, the Báb and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, with reported talks and recorded accounts among them; supplied wording, including letters written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi and of the Universal House of Justice, follows at the end with its catalogue status.

Bahá’u’lláh writes, Teach ye the Cause of God, O people of Bahá, for God hath prescribed unto every one the duty of proclaiming His Message, and regardeth it as the most meritorious of all deeds. Elsewhere He says the obligation has been imposed upon every one, and bids His loved ones repose not on their couches but unloose their tongues. In His Will and Testament ‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls teaching the greatest of all the gifts of God and our first obligation, the head corner-stone of the foundation itself. His Tablets ask each friend to teach at least one soul within a year, and tell one who could not decide between writing and teaching that for the present teaching is preferable. Why do the Writings make teaching the duty of every believer rather than of a few? What do the provisions for those unable to speak suggest about what the duty asks?

These readings consider what teaching is worth. The Báb writes that it is better to guide one soul than to possess all that is on earth, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá recalls the saying, O ‘Alí! If God guide, through thee, one soul, it is better for thee than all the riches. Bahá’u’lláh calls the command to teach the greatest and most mighty after the recognition of God, citing the verse that whoso quickens a soul is as though he had quickened all humanity, and He calls His loved ones the world’s spiritual physicians. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá names the station of a teacher the greatest of all stations, and compares the herald of the Kingdom to a farmer whose station is raised in the estimation of the lord of the village. Images of increase recur: the lamp from which lamp after lamp is lit, the one who plants trees that others may benefit, the chain through which one holy soul becomes the cause of life to a hundred thousand. Reported talks speak of the joy that teaching brings. Why is the guidance of a single soul weighed against all the riches of the earth? What does the image of the chain add to it?

Images of increase recur: the lamp from which lamp after lamp is lit, the one who plants trees that others may benefit, the chain through which one holy soul becomes the cause of life to a hundred thousand. Reported talks speak of the joy that teaching brings. Why is the guidance of a single soul weighed against all the riches of the earth? What does the image of the chain add to it?

These readings turn to the instruments of teaching. Bahá’u’lláh says that to assist Him is to teach His Cause, and that although He could render the Cause victorious through a single word, He has ordained that complete victory be achieved through speech and utterance; the decree of holy war by the sword has been lifted. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls utterance the world-conquering sword of the friends, a sword that taketh not life but bestoweth it. Wisdom governs its use. Bahá’u’lláh asks that one speak to each soul according to its capacity, that the earth first be made receptive and then the word delivered, and He says that one who cries out for people to rend their veils is not counted among the teachers; wisdom, He explains, means such deeds as cause the heedless to become aware. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá adds that wisdom is steadfastness in teaching, not silence and fear, and counsels gentle speech and argument in the most excellent manner. A reported talk warns against thrusting the teachings on unwilling listeners. How can wisdom restrain speech without becoming an excuse for silence? What makes a word attract rather than repel?

Why must friendship be genuine rather than a method?

These readings look inward, at the one who teaches. Bahá’u’lláh says that unless the heart is detached words have no effect, and that when the teacher is enkindled with the fire of His love and adorned with detachment, his words will set ablaze those that hear him. He asks His servants to speak for the sake of God and to look not to rejection or acceptance but to the service they have been bidden. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that we must first remember ourselves and then turn to others, for one who has not found existence cannot bestow it, and that one who has taught himself will be able to teach others. He describes travellers who went seeking fame and fortune and returned utterly disappointed, and a reported talk says confirmations do not accompany those who would gather a group around themselves. Teaching is called a gift of God, not a matter of talent or learning, and Bahá’u’lláh tells one who lacked outward learning not to grieve. The Báb asks that one journey only if no sorrow is found in the heart. What does detachment mean for a teacher in practice? Why would motive change the effect of the same words?

These readings concern the one who hears. Bahá’u’lláh says that if one is found who thirsts he should be given the pure wine, and otherwise it should be preserved in its vessel; if one is receptive, cast upon him the melodies of the Spirit, and if he turns away, turn unto God. He suggests approaches for different hearers: prominent people who will lead others troop after troop, the gatherings of the Theosophical Society, and an official coming little by little to believe. Reported talks advise speaking to the irreligious of what distinguishes humans from the animal kingdom, and recall the seed that fell by the wayside. Should response lessen, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes, be not saddened, for we are commanded to sow and the growth rests with God. How can a teacher discern readiness without judging others? What does the farmer’s patience teach?

These readings record the limits that circumstances placed on teaching. What distinguishes prudence from fear?

These readings speak of the assistance promised to those who teach. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that whoever arises to herald the Kingdom produces a magnetic power which attracts the rays of confirmation, and that one who is steadfast and arises with all his power will find himself assisted by the angels of heaven and the hosts of the Concourse on high. Difficulty is expected: every great cause must needs have its difficulties, and though India is slow to respond, the friends are not to be discouraged. Why are the promises of assistance tied so closely to arising? What do these readings suggest about the place of difficulty?

Victory, He says, is of two kinds: the conquest of strongholds is easy, but the conquest of hearts is difficult save through the power of the Most Great Name. Reported talks describe confirmation as the net and unity as the bait, and say that no capacity is limited when led by the Spirit of God. Difficulty is expected: every great cause must needs have its difficulties, and though India is slow to respond, the friends are not to be discouraged. Why are the promises of assistance tied so closely to arising? What do these readings suggest about the place of difficulty?

These readings turn to the ways teachers are prepared and teaching is arranged. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls teaching gatherings and study classes supremely confirmed, asks the friends to study the lessons of teaching and memorize the sacred Tablets, and, observing that teachers are few while the cry rises, Where is the teacher?, asks that every city establish teaching classes for the young. He warns that years spent first on syntax and rhetoric would lose the opportunity. Bahá’u’lláh asks that several souls in every city gather to consult about teaching, and that in every land the friends appoint a teacher and provide for his needs through an unnamed intermediary. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá also insists that at that stage promotion came before organization: the time for order will come, but now is not the time, and committees that yield no result are not the aim. Meetings are to be in ecstasy, with prayers, Tablets, proofs and news from other parts, and to be continual rather than scattered. Why does He put promotion before organization? What would a gathering that teaches look like in your own community?

These readings follow teachers on the road. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá tells one teacher not to stay more than nineteen days in any city, and says teachers should, as Christ said, shake the very dust of a city from their shoes on leaving it. A reported saying holds that in movement there is life and in immobility death. In the Tablets of the Divine Plan He asks the believers of North America to travel themselves or to send others throughout the states, to let their exertions increase a thousandfold, and to carry the call to other parts of the world, recalling how the few firm souls in the lifetime of Christ were followed by countless souls beneath the shadow of the Gospel. Other Tablets encourage journeys to the Caucasus, to Paris, to the Hawaiian Islands and among the tribes. Bahá’u’lláh sets a limit: it is not permissible to insist that anyone travel to teach. Why do the Writings attribute such power to movement? How does the counsel against insisting shape the call to arise?

These readings gather accounts of those who taught. A recorded account gives the Báb’s words bidding a follower to be engaged in a mosque in prayer and in teaching. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá tells of a believer led about the streets with a halter who, composed and smiling, kept on speaking to the people, and of another who, bound in chains, never wavered in teaching. He recalls Paul, who after severe beatings arose and proclaimed the Cause in the nearby city, and Bahá’u’lláh recalls that Peter was a fisher of fish and Abu Dharr a shepherd. Reported talks tell of an illiterate man in Persia who guided many great men through his pure love of God, a village woman who in one year lit forty lamps, and a man who resolved to hunt souls rather than animals. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá also describes His own journeys: in a reported talk He recalls that, weary in America, He would first concentrate on the Blessed Beauty and then His voice would be raised, and a Tablet recalls His going to Montreal though warned against it. What do these lives have in common? Which example speaks most directly to your own circumstances?

The guide closes with prayers for teaching. Bahá’u’lláh trusts that God will aid Him and His servants to exalt His name, to deliver His Message and to proclaim His Cause, and asks to be assisted so to teach that the dead may speed out of their sepulchers and rush forth towards God. In another prayer He says that, though the lover be loth to share with any one the intimate conversation of his beloved, whenever the commandment to declare the Cause reaches Him He will unhesitatingly obey it, undeterred by the darts of affliction. Other prayers ask to arise with bared head and cry out God’s name amidst His creatures, and recall arising, when His summons came, to call all in heaven and earth to His favors. A prayer of the Báb in a recorded account asks that the infant seed of God may soon germinate in the hearts of men and grow into a mighty tree beneath whose shadow all peoples may gather. How do these prayers join the inner life of devotion to the outward work of teaching? Which of their requests could become a daily prayer?

questions: The readings call teaching both the duty of every believer and the greatest gift of God. How do the sections on the call and on its reward fit together? Is a gift something one can be commanded to receive?

Bahá’u’lláh lifts the decree of the sword and ordains victory through utterance, yet many passages say deeds exert greater influence than words. How do utterance and deeds work together in the readings, and where would you place the warning that kindliness used only to convert is hypocrisy?

Several readings say to give the wine to the thirsty and otherwise keep it in its vessel, while others say to let no opportunity pass. How do the readings on receptive soil and on wisdom help a teacher hold these together?

The section on prudence records lands where teaching was forbidden or concealed. What do these passages show about wisdom, and how do they differ from the silence, fear and dread that ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says wisdom is not?

Many passages promise confirmation to those who arise, and others describe difficulty, slow response and weariness. Using the examples of Paul, the believer led with a halter, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s own journeys, consider what the readings say confirmation does and does not mean.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá puts promotion before organization, praises study classes and consultation, and asks each friend to befriend one soul a year. What would these counsels look like if a small group of friends in one neighborhood tried to follow them together?
